title: Short Fart
blurb: Three tenths of a second, start to finish. This is the smallest unit of fart currently in circulation: one dry, airy pip with a sharp attack and no tail whatsoever. Brevity is the whole design. Because it ends before anyone can react, it works as pure punctuation — a comma where the loud versions are exclamation marks. Editors slip it between cuts or fire it twice for a double take, and on a Discord soundboard it is the polite option, insofar as that word applies to anything here. Blink and the joke has already happened without you.
origin: A generic short fart recording; no specific source.

title: Premium Fart
blurb: The premium in question is build quality. On a spectrogram this clip shows a flutter so regular it could pass an engineering inspection: eight tenths of a second of tight, evenly spaced sputter, then a clean stop with no trailing wheeze. It sounds expensive the way a well-tuned two-stroke engine sounds expensive. Use it when the joke calls for competence rather than chaos, or lay it under an unboxing video at the exact moment the packaging opens. Of all the farts on this page, this is the one you could imagine shipping with a warranty card.
origin: A stock fart recording circulated under the 'premium fart' name.

title: Funny Fart
blurb: A beat of silence, one squeaky honk, and out. The comedy here is register: this fart sits noticeably higher than its neighbours, closer to a party balloon being pinched at the neck than to anything bass-driven. High-pitched farts read as accidents rather than statements, and accidents are funnier. It also arrives slightly late in its own file, which gives the button a built-in comic pause when you press it live. Good under pratfalls, dropped phones, and anybody bending over on camera. Of the squeak family, this is the standard-issue model, and it has never needed improving.

title: Burst Fart
blurb: One single swell, like a balloon deflating through a trombone. This take blooms from nothing, peaks around the half-second mark and rolls off gently, with none of the sputter texture fans expect from the genre. The shape matters: because it fades rather than stopping dead, it leaves space for a reaction shot, and editors use that gap constantly. Think of it as the legato fart — the smooth alternative to the staccato pops elsewhere on this page. It suits slow-motion footage, deflating-confidence montages, and any scene that was already heading downhill before the audio arrived.

title: Proud Fart
blurb: Announced rather than released. This one opens at full volume, takes a breath halfway through and pushes on to a second peak, which is the acoustic equivalent of making eye contact while it happens. There is no apology anywhere in the waveform. A steady, brassy midrange gives it the bearing of a short trumpet voluntary, and the two-stage delivery makes it feel rehearsed. Use it for triumphs played completely straight: a promotion email, a difficult parallel park, a boss kill. No other button on this hub would take a bow, and this one is already bowing.
origin: A generic fart recording with a notably assertive two-stage delivery.

title: Hype Fart
blurb: Somebody built a drop around it. The first five seconds are pure festival riser: a sweep climbing steadily in pitch, tension stacking exactly the way it does before any bass drop you have ever heard. Then a beat of dead silence. Then the fart, carrying the full weight of everything the build promised. The structure only has one joke, but the ear falls for the riser afresh on each listen, so it keeps landing. Play it whole; skipping ahead dismantles the machine. Best over sports edits, reveal videos, and countdowns to things that were never going to be good.
origin: A fart edited onto a DJ-style riser build-up; the underlying recording is generic.

title: Juicy Fart
blurb: Not one fart but a recital. Seven seconds contain a hissing overture, a volley of quick pops, a fat middle movement, and a finale that sputters through more textures than seems anatomically advisable. The juicy label describes the mastering as much as the material: this file runs noticeably hotter than its neighbours, with the moisture pushed right to the front of the mix. Fail compilations reach for this class of audio when one blast cannot carry a whole timeline. Warn anyone on headphones before you press it, or don't, depending entirely on the relationship.
origin: A generic multi-part fart recording, mastered loud.

title: Perfect Fart
blurb: Perfection at this length is a matter of proportion. A third of a second, a rounded attack, a tidy tail: every stage of this fart is present and in the correct ratio, like a scale model of a much larger event. Where the short fart on this page is a dry pip, this one is a complete note with a beginning, a middle and an end. That completeness is what editors want when a clip has to read instantly on a phone speaker in a noisy feed. It is the take you choose when the joke must be finished before the scroll moves on.
origin: A generic fart recording; no film or viral moment behind it.

title: Long Brain Fart
blurb: Twelve seconds is a very long time. This marathon take simply refuses to end: six distinct movements, a peak somewhere in the middle, and a closing run of evenly spaced pops that lands like a drum fill wrapping up a solo. Nobody needs a fart this long, and the running time itself becomes the punchline somewhere around second eight. The title files it under the brain fart family of meme sounds; the audio is a fart with unusual stamina. Let it run under end credits, or use it to fill an awkward silence so completely that the silence apologises.
origin: An extended fart recording circulated under the 'brain fart' name.

title: Brain Fart with Reverb
blurb: Where this hub's other reverb fart throws one clean note into a cathedral, this one throws a whole sputtering phrase into the room and lets the walls sort it out. The result is murkier and stranger: reflections smear the individual pops into a haunted rumble, and the tail keeps whispering for a full second after the source stops. It sounds less like architecture and more like a stairwell at midnight. Reach for it in horror-parody edits, or anywhere a fart needs to feel like an event being witnessed from a different floor of the building.
origin: A 'brain fart' style recording with added reverb.

title: Gahdayum Fart
blurb: The reaction is included in the price. A voice gets half a word out before the blast takes over, a two-second ripper with genuine sustain, and then the verdict arrives: a drawled gahh-dayum of the sort normally reserved for barbecue and highlight reels. Bundling commentary with catastrophe saves editors a job, since one file now supplies both the event and its audience. It plays best over footage of somebody else's mistake, where the drawl does the judging on your behalf. Three and a half seconds, and a complete piece of radio drama.
origin: A fart clip bundled with a drawled 'gahdayum' reaction; the performers are unknown.

title: I Have to Let One Rip
blurb: Forty seconds of build-up for one second of payoff. Most of this file is somebody narrating the predicament in the title, the delivery growing more strained as the situation develops, and the release only arrives in the final moment, after the audience has abandoned all hope of it. As soundboard economics go this is absurd, and the absurdity is the appeal: nobody expects a fart clip with a three-act structure. Play it in a call and make the whole room sit through the full negotiation. The length is the prank, and pressing stop early is cowardice.
origin: A comedy monologue clip that ends in the promised fart; the performer is uncredited.

title: Bark Fart
blurb: Two clipped bursts, a breath apart, in precisely the rhythm of a small dog objecting to a doorbell. The resemblance is the whole act. Heard cold, people genuinely hesitate over which animal they are dealing with, and the wrong guess is funnier every time it happens. The double-tap shape also unlocks uses a single blast cannot manage: call and response, or a knock at a door that should not be answered. Pair it with actual dog footage and the dog takes the blame, which is the oldest deflection in the history of the genre. Nothing else here covers this register.
origin: A generic fart recording whose two-burst rhythm resembles a dog bark.

title: Loud Fart During Church
blurb: Context comes baked into the recording. The first half is hush: a low, organ-toned ambience, a few small shuffles, the unmistakable sound of a large stone room being respectful. Then the fart detonates into all that reverence, and the building's own echo carries it considerably further than anybody present would have wanted. You can hear the room in the tail, long and stony. Because the setting travels with the file, one press delivers the entire scenario — sacrilege included, no editing required. Deploy it wherever the solemnity has become unbearable. Somebody, somewhere, clearly reached the same conclusion.
origin: A recording of a loud fart in a reverberant church-like setting; the source is unknown.

title: Fahhh Earrape
blurb: There was, it turns out, headroom above the loud version. This edit removes it: the level sits within a decibel of full scale for the entire file, every sample slammed against the digital ceiling until the scream is more distortion than voice. Earrape is a genre with exactly one convention, honoured here completely. The hub's very loud edition at least preserves the shape of the original recording; this one preserves only the hostility. Turn something down before you test it. Played on yourself it is a mistake, and played on a friend it is, apparently, content.
origin: A heavily clipped earrape edit of the viral Taileons 'fahhh' scream.

title: Slow Fahhh
blurb: Slowing the scream changes what it means. At reduced speed the panic drains out and something closer to grief seeps in: the pitch drops, the vowel stretches past the original clip's entire running time, and the result lands like disappointment played at its correct emotional tempo. Slowed edits traditionally get paired with reverb and captions about being tired, and this one arrives ready for that lane. It suits losses that deserve dignity rather than chaos — the missed flight, the deleted save file. Underneath, the Taileons recording is untouched; it has simply been made to feel everything for longer.
origin: The Taileons 'fahhh' scream, slowed and pitched down.

title: Fahhh Pump Sound
blurb: A thump on the front, then the grind. This edit opens with a percussive hit and drags the scream out behind it as a low, distorted drone, bass boosted until the vowel stops being a vowel and starts being machinery. The steady growl underneath points the whole thing at gym-edit territory, where audio gets judged on menace per second. Whatever the pump in the title refers to, this is the most mechanical shape the scream has yet been bent into. Run it under lifting montages, engine footage, or any moment of deeply serious effort that deserves undermining.
origin: A bass-heavy, distorted edit of the viral 'fahhh' scream.

title: Riley Fahhh Remix
blurb: Somebody sat down and produced this properly. Ten seconds of actual arrangement: a beat, a low end, and the fahhh scream chopped into the grid as lead instrument, triggered on rhythm as though it came from a legitimate sample pack. Turning a meme scream into music is a tradition as old as meme screams themselves, and this entry brings more craft than the genre strictly demands. Who Riley is, the file does not say; the name arrived attached to the remix and stayed. Unlike the raw versions, it genuinely works as a loop for intros and starting-soon screens.
origin: A fan-made musical remix of the viral 'fahhh' scream, circulated under the name Riley.

title: HHHAF
blurb: Read the title backwards and you have understood the file. This is the fahhh scream reversed from start to finish: instead of a bang that decays, you get a whisper that swells, gathering menace for two seconds and then cutting off dead at what used to be the beginning. Reversed audio has carried horror connotations for as long as tape machines have existed, and the trick works even on a meme scream — the crescendo feels like something approaching at speed. Play this, then the original, and the pair becomes a slingshot. The spelling is the honest part.
origin: The viral 'fahhh' scream played in reverse.
